https://en.tempo.co/read/2117286/hungary.text: TEMPO.CO, Jakarta - Hungary's parliament voted in Andras Baka, formerly the head of the Supreme Court, as the country's next president on Tuesday. The symbolic step is part of new Prime Minister Peter Magyar's sweeping efforts to dismantle the legacy of former premier Viktor Orban after winning April's general elections. Baka was a staunch critic of Orban who was removed from his Supreme Court role during the former PM's tenure. Now, he will replace Tamas Sulyok, a president appointed by Orban, whose term in office was shortened via constitutional amendment in order to remove him from the largely ceremonial role. What happened in Tuesday's parliamentary vote? The vote in parliament to appoint Baka was always likely to be a formality, given the massive majority that Magyar's conservative, pro-European TISZA party holds in the chamber. It went almost entirely along party lines, 140 lawmakers voted in favor and six voted against. TISZA holds 141 seats. Orban's right-wing populist Fidesz party, which has 52 lawmakers, boycotted the vote in protest — but did so knowing it would be powerless to prevent Baka's appointment.Who is Andras Baka? Baka, 73, is a jurist and politician who was briefly a member of parliament from 1990 to 1991. He spent almost 20 years as a judge at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), before returning to Hungary in 2009 to become president of its Supreme Court. In December 2011, not long after Orban returned to power as prime minister after a stint in opposition, he was removed from his role three years before his term was set to expire and sidelined from public life in Hungary. Magyar said Baka's life served "as an example of commitment to the democratic rule of law and constitutional principles" as the central European country needs to be "guided back onto the path of the rule of law and constitutional governance."Why was Baka's appointment and his predecessor's removal contentious? Baka's appointment prompted protests from Fidesz, but also some critical comments elsewhere in Hungary, with some rights watchdogs likening the removal of Tamas Sulyok to the "illiberal" practices of the Orban-era. Sulyok, appointed in 2024, was deemed an Orban ally. Magyar used his two-thirds majority in parliament — which he holds thanks to Hungary's winner-takes-all first-past-the-post electoral system, as Orban used to — to amend the constitution and bring his term to an early end. Fidesz and their nationalist KDNP allies in parliament had called this "tyrannical" and "illegitimate," while Magyar argued it was necessary to pursue the "system change" he promised amid April's landslide election victory. Magyar briefly tapped Hungarian national treasure and chess superstar Judit Polgar as a possible replacement president, but she quickly declined, saying she did not feel she had "the strength to take on the historic responsibility of uniting a divided nation," but pledging to do "everything in my power" to support a new, independent and respected president.What has Baka said about the process and his appointment? Baka himself had not criticized Sulyok's removal, despite the echoes of the mechanisms used to oust him in 2011. "In a country governed by the rule of law, such extraordinary measures cannot be used, but Hungary became a captured state under Orban," he told the AFP news agency last month. He said that state officials like Sulyok "were appointed not to restrain the government's power, but to ensure the political survival of the former system even after an electoral defeat." However, speaking in parliament on Tuesday, Baka seemed to strike a conciliatory tone, even for supporters of the old regime."There is one thing we certainly cannot do: we cannot build the new Hungary on revenge," he told parliament, vowing to "encourage public and professional debate, uphold [parliament's] openness and impartiality, and consistently insist that constitution-making must never again become the exclusive project of a single political force."Read: Europe's Rivers Are Drying Up: Can They Be Saved?Click here to get the latest news updates from Tempo on Google News

The bus ran into a ditch and tipped over early on Sunday ​near the town of Mezokeresztes in eastern Hungary, police said, ​adding that the bus was heading towards the city of ⁠Nyiregyhaza on the motorway when the accident happened. State news agency MTI ​said there were 57 passengers and two drivers on the bus. Pictures ​from the scene showed a badly damaged red bus lying on one side in a ditch by the motorway with windows smashed and belongings and suitcases scattered ​around. "A Polish-registered bus travelling on the M3 motorway towards Nyiregyhaza ... veered ​off the straight stretch of road into a ditch and overturned. Preliminary information suggests ‌the ⁠driver likely fell asleep," police said on their website. Polish President Karol Nawrocki said on X: "It is with deep sorrow that I received the tragic news of the Polish bus accident in Hungary, in which so ​many of our ​compatriots died." Twelve ⁠people lost their lives and several others were injured in the accident, police said, adding that they were ​taking the bus driver into custody. The injured have been ​taken to ⁠hospital. Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said on X that a "tragic accident" involving a bus carrying Polish tourists happened in Hungary. "The consular service is operational. ⁠We ​are in contact with the Hungarian authorities. ​The Ministry of Foreign Affairs will provide verified information," he said. https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text: OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, said the company had ‘learned our lesson’. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters View image in fullscreen OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, said the company had ‘learned our lesson’. Photograph: Hollie Adams/Reuters OpenAI Analysis OpenAI delivers a mea culpa to the Australian government in person – but answers still elude Josh Butler Jason Kwon’s answers were provided in a helpful, quiet and calm manner. For a company under intense scrutiny, there were no missteps Tue 6 Oct 2026 07.12 EDT Share Open AI’s Jason Kwon flew 15 hours from San Francisco to Sydney to give the company’s first in-person mea culpa after it admitted – in an unsigned email, to a public departmental inbox – that one of its AI agents had accessed a Services Australia website without authorisation and grabbed data related to Medicare. Kwon – polite, friendly, even-toned – got through a potentially dicey committee hearing unscathed, promising to do better and pledging assistance to Australia. No missteps, no viral moments, just delivering his answers helpfully, in a quiet and calm manner, sympathising with the questioner and the point they were making. In other words, just like ChatGPT. Even the content of his responses evoked the AI assistant he was there to defend. 1:18 OpenAI admits misstep in handling AI agent interactions with Australian government sites – video Asked by Pocock “why did you send an email to an arbitrary department email?” Kwon replied: “In retrospect, we should have done what you’re suggesting”. Asked why Altman wasn’t informed before his meeting with Marles, and why the company didn’t fess up there, Kwon said: “I agree the process by which people became aware of this incident inside our company could have been much better”. One couldn’t help but be reminded of the way the chatbot responds when pulled up on a mistake: “Good catch. You’re right to push back. My bad, that one’s on me.” In Kwon’s parlance, the models – built from the ground up by OpenAI , which reportedly wants to value itself at $1.4tn – “accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not directed to.” He tried to explain that the “novelty” of this incident meant the company had “learned our lesson”, which was that it should inform victims of such incidents much earlier, rather than waiting. Kwon again apologised for the company only sending a casual email to the federal government disclosing that its agent had inappropriately accessed Medicare statistics , but tried to explain to Tuesday’s parliamentary hearing that it was sometimes “difficult” to figure how to make such notifications to a big sprawling public service. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Senator David Pocock helpfully offered: “I assume someone in your government relations team has mobile phone numbers of ministers and various people?” There was a similar air of post-facto contrition as Kwon – OpenAI’s chief strategy officer – could offer few answers about why the company’s CEO, Sam Altman, didn’t inform the Australian deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, about the incident when they met face-to-face in San Francisco on 1 September. That was nine days before the company emailed Services Australia, and nearly a whole month after it first learned of the 18 June intrusion. Kwon said Altman wasn’t aware of the incident before the Marles meeting. After today’s committee hearing , it’s still unclear why. It’s a big government, and maybe Kwon is right that it’s “difficult” to find the right person to talk to. But some could also argue that your boss shaking hands with Australia’s deputy prime minister would be something of a useful window. At least, we learned, he said the company didn’t use AI to write the infamous email. Small blessings that they managed to ask a human to write the email – even if it went to an obscure inbox. But with Australia actually striving to become a tech capital for datacentres and AI – as the revolving door of big tech companies told the inquiry, from Anthropic to Microsoft and Google – then setting the basic rules of the road for these firms, about how they must act and respond to this country and its government, is critical. Kwon said OpenAI was committed to providing future notifications “very quickly”, and that there were no further incidents they were aware of. But he casually dropped in one staggering fact: OpenAI was still trawling through the activity logs for the agents involved in the Services Australia breach, with those logs totalling 50 petabytes of data. A petabyte is 1,000 terabytes, or 1 million gigabytes. Kwon made the mind-boggling claim that it would take a human 66m years – never sleeping, never resting – to go through that data by hand. The team tasked with checking Services Australia’s email inboxes must be hoping there aren’t any more dramas lurking in there. https://www.wsws.org/en/articles/2026/09.text: Menu Search Latest Profile English Contact | About | International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Menu Search International Committee of the Fourth International ( ICFI ) Latest Profile Fourth International Socialist Equality Party IYSSE About the WSWS Contact Donate “We are NOT cannon fodder!” Young people in Essen strike against conscription on December 5, 2025 On Friday, school students in more than a hundred German cities took strike action against conscription for the fourth time. Recent weeks have shown just how important this fight is, as Germany escalates a war against Russia at an unprecedented pace. Conscription is being introduced so that we young people can serve as cannon fodder in this war. The German government is implementing the largest rearmament programme since the Second World War. The Bundeswehr is to become the strongest army in Europe. NATO has agreed to raise defence spending to 5 percent of GDP by 2035. Berlin is permanently stationing an armoured brigade in Lithuania, close to the border with Russia and Belarus. The weapons Kiev uses are financed, jointly developed and often directly supplied by NATO. In close cooperation with the German government and the other NATO powers, Ukraine is carrying out attacks deep inside Russian territory—on energy facilities and infrastructure, with residential buildings also being hit. Only a few days ago, during the Russian Duma elections, the heaviest drone attack yet struck Moscow . Russia, in turn, is intensifying its attacks on Ukraine. On both sides, it is workers who bear the cost. This must be said openly: Germany is once again, in effect, at war with Russia. Russian retaliatory strikes are not merely accepted as a risk, but deliberately provoked. Every incident serves as a justification for ever more direct NATO intervention. In early August, without presenting any solid evidence, the German government blamed Moscow for a drone found near Leipzig Airport . It immediately stepped up its propaganda to rally the population behind its war course. Russian consulates and cultural institutions were closed, severing diplomatic and cultural ties built up over decades. The government cannot secure fast enough the cannon fodder it needs for this war. By its own timetable, nationwide conscription medical examinations were not due to begin until July 2027, yet more than 1,000 young men in Kiel and Flensburg have already been summoned to one, many of them having stated explicitly on their registration forms that they had no interest in military service. One of them was told by phone that police would come if he again refused to attend. At the same time, Defence Minister Boris Pistorius (Social Democratic Party, SPD) has announced that soldiers will be compelled to serve in the Lithuania brigade so that it is ready for deployment by the end of 2027. This makes clear just how serious the question of conscription is. It is not simply a matter of spending a year in barracks. We are to be drafted into the Bundeswehr—if necessary, against our will—and stationed on the eastern front, where the government is now igniting an open war. Workers and young people are being made to pay twice over for this war: with their lives at the front—and with higher prices, crumbling schools, universities and hospitals starved of funding, and with cuts to youth clubs and social benefits. The hundreds of billions of euros spent on tanks and drones are missing everywhere they are needed. Rearmament means social cuts. What is this war about? According to the government and its media mouthpieces, rearmament is necessary to defend “democracy” and “freedom” against the Russian threat. But this is a propaganda lie. The war in Ukraine is not about defence, but about the economic and geopolitical interests of German capital: access to raw materials and labour in Russia and Ukraine, huge profits for the arms industry, and the control and subjugation of Russia and the entire former Soviet Union. The Putin regime’s invasion of Ukraine was reactionary and must be condemned. But it was the reaction of the Russian oligarchy to decades of NATO’s eastward expansion, through which the country was systematically encircled. In the 20th century, German imperialism has already marched eastward twice. In the Second World War, Hitler waged a barbaric war of annihilation against the Soviet Union, in which at least 27 million Soviet citizens lost their lives and the Jews of Europe were systematically murdered. Today, more than 80 years after the defeat of the Nazi regime, Berlin is reviving this tradition. And it is doing so in collaboration with a regime in Kiev that venerates the Nazi collaborators of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN) and the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) as “national heroes” and integrates fascist forces into the state and the army. This is no coincidence, but a deliberate programme. The war has already cost hundreds of thousands of young people their lives on both sides. In Ukraine, armed squads from the recruitment authorities drive through the streets, seizing men to be thrown into the meat grinder at the front. Around 2 million Ukrainians are evading conscription, and at least 200,000 soldiers have deserted. Spontaneous protests against forced recruitment keep breaking out. The German government is actively assisting Kiev in this. Foreign Minister Wadephul wants to hand over the data of Ukrainian refugees of military age living in Germany to Kiev and have them swiftly deported. The case of Bogdan Syrotiuk There is no democracy in Ukraine, only a dictatorship. The case of the Ukrainian socialist Bogdan Syrotiuk proves this. On August 10, he was sentenced by a Ukrainian court to 15 years in prison—not for any crime, but because he wrote articles against war and fascism. The court also ordered his socialist books and documents be destroyed. Bogdan is an opponent of the Putin regime and the Russian invasion, just as he is an opponent of NATO’s warmongers and the Zelensky regime. In his articles, he exposed how Nazi collaborators such as Stepan Bandera are glorified in Ukraine. The Young Guard of Bolshevik-Leninists, a Trotskyist youth organisation he founded, called for the unity of Russian and Ukrainian workers against their respective governments. For this, he is to spend 15 years in prison. Given his poor state of health and the catastrophic conditions in Ukrainian prisons, this amounts to a death sentence. Bogdan’s persecution is not an isolated case. Since the 2014 Maidan coup, Ukraine has banned left-wing parties, no elections have been held, strikes are prohibited, and critical media such as the World Socialist Web Site have been blocked. The German government and mainstream media outlets stay silent about this, including about Bogdan’s persecution, even though his case has even been accepted by the European Court of Human Rights. Bogdan’s freedom can only be won by workers and young people. His fight is our fight. We are to be thrown into the very war he opposes and the crackdown on opponents of the war is growing ever harsher. Why the Left Party and the AfD are no alternative Anger at the war and austerity policies of the federal government is enormous, which is proven by the recent state elections. But the beneficiaries were two parties that are themselves parties of war: the Left Party and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). Socialism AI by the WSWS SocialismAI.com Questions about this article? Ask Socialism AI What happened during the 2014 Maidan coup, and how did it lead to the banning of left-wing parties in Ukraine? What is the historical origin of the Fourth International's Trotskyist movement, and how does it differ from Stalinism in its analysis of war and nationalism? How does the current German rearmament drive connect to Germany's historical role in the two world wars, and what does that history suggest about where this trajectory leads? Ask more questions at SocialismAI.com The Left Party, the election winner in Berlin , talks left and acts right. Its predecessor, the PDS, helped carry through the reintroduction of capitalism in East Germany after 1990 and later cut social spending in Berlin and Thuringia. Despite its rhetoric about peace, the Left Party voted in the upper chamber of parliament in favour of billions of euros in rearmament spending for the Bundeswehr and backed NATO’s confrontation with Russia. It is not an anti-war party but a party of German imperialism wearing a “left” mask. If the Left Party goes on to lead the Berlin Senate (state legislature), it will carry out the same policy of cuts that it criticised during the election campaign. In doing so, it is paving the way for the far right. The AfD, which became the strongest party in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, is no “peace party” or alternative “from below,” but the most aggressive representative of the policy of war and the dictatorship of the financial oligarchy. It was the first to call for raising military spending to 5 percent of GDP and wants to massively build up the state apparatus. It scapegoats refugees for the social catastrophe and divides the working class with its nationalist agitation. The AfD has been systematically promoted and built up by the government, the media and the state apparatus in order to channel opposition to war and social cuts into right-wing dead ends and brutally suppress it. And the trade unions? In the fight over wages and jobs, they stand on the side of the corporations. In early September, behind the backs of the workforce, IG Metall agreed to the destruction of 75,000 jobs at Volkswagen . Four plants face closure. The German Trade Union Confederation (DGB) and its member unions suppress every act of resistance to war and cuts—and in doing so are driving workers into the arms of the AfD. That is why the working class needs its own party, one that breaks with all the bourgeois parties and stands on an independent, revolutionary programme. This is what we in the International Youth and Students for Social Equality (IYSSE), the youth organisation of the Sozialistische Gleichheitspartei (Socialist Equality Party, SGP), are fighting for. What perspective in the fight against war? Ukraine is not an isolated theatre of war but part of an escalating world war with further fronts in the Middle East—from the genocide in Gaza to the war against Iran. The deep contradictions of world capitalism are once again driving all the imperialist powers toward a violent redivision of the world. It is a race for resources, influence and profits—waged on the backs of the workers. This world war and the introduction of conscription can only be stopped by an international movement of the working class fighting for the overthrow of capitalism. This is the socialist perspective for which Bogdan stands. Workers and young people of all countries must reject nationalism and unite in the struggle against their own governments, rather than being driven into war against one another. “Only internationalism, not bourgeois or petty-bourgeois nationalism, can end poverty, oppression and injustice,” Bogdan declared in his speech marking May Day 2023. Our allies are not to be found in parliament, but in the factories, schools and universities—in Germany, Russia, Ukraine and around the world. There is no time to lose. Join the fight for socialism!
